utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have a number of matters to deal with before the next witness is called. The first one relates to protective measures for Witness W-50. The Prosecution had requested a pseudonym, image and voice distortion for this witness. On the 7th of February, the Trial Chamber delayed its decision on the request and required the Prosecution to provide further and more recent information on the witness's circumstances and the reasons for requesting protective measures. We have not yet received this information and the witness is scheduled to testify this afternoon. The Prosecution should, therefore, provide the Chamber with the information. The next matter relates to a confidential motion for admission into evidence of written statements pursuant to 92 ter. This is an application for four witnesses. The Defence responded on the 19th of February, objecting to the admission of the statements under what it described as the time conditions proposed by the Prosecution, stating that it defers to the decision of the Chamber and applies for the allocation of reasonable time-limits for cross-examination of these witnesses. The Chamber will allocate reasonable time for cross-examination based on the factors identified in its oral ruling of the 14th of February. The Chamber therefore grants the Prosecution's motion and admits the statements of Witnesses W-38, W-57, W-91 and W-116. We'll decide on the time for cross-examination when the witnesses are scheduled to appear. The parties will recall that I have, time and again, raised the question of certain witnesses being called by the Trial Chamber. This is because the Chamber takes the view that these witnesses are needed to attend at the trial in the interests of the administration of justice. However, before the Chamber issues a summons for these witnesses to appear, the Chamber considers it appropriate to invite the Prosecution to call these witnesses. Accordingly, Mr. Whiting, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to call Captain Hansen as well as the unidentified officer of the UNMO who heard and saw the projectile in flight from a particular direction. Mr. Whiting, the Chamber will expect to be kept abreast of the progress being made in this matter on a weekly basis, and we'd like to have the first report by Monday of next week. I must -- yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I can report right now that we have been endeavouring to identify the unidentified UNMO officer. We're working on that. We have been working on that quite diligently. Hopefully by next Monday I will have more specific information to report on that effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would not want this matter to be stretched over time. I would want this witness to be here as soon as possible, the reason being that I take the view that it is better to hear this witness when the issues are live and fresh in the minds of everyone in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the same view. We've been working on it as diligently as we can. It's been a little bit difficult and I cannot guarantee that we will ultimately be able to identify that person. So far we've been unsuccessful. The most obvious way of identifying that person has not been successful, that is, asking the person who spoke with him and reported about the conversation. He does not remember, but we're working on it to see if we can identify him. But we will try to make this happen as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can get Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then, get Captain Hansen, because you don't have to bring the two of them at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if that's fine with you, we can make that arrangement. It's not our view that he has significantly more to contribute than has been already presented to the Trial Chamber, but now that the Trial Chamber has invited us to bring him, I think we will probably do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You'll recall that at one of the sittings last week there was a divergence of opinion in the translation of a particular passage, and I instructed the registrar to have the CLSS review the translation and provide with us a translation. I have received the translation and I'll read it to the parties. This comes from Christina Zoric, Chief, CLSS. They referred to the B/C/S original, which I will not read or, more accurately, I cannot read, and the English translation they say should read: "The bullet passed through the child's head and then seriously wounded his mother in the stomach." At the time when I requested the court deputy to have this translation done by the CLSS, I also indicated that I would allow the parties to make any short submissions that they might have arising from the translation received from the CLSS. Accordingly, I do so now. So I ask, first -- well, I ask first the Prosecutor whether he has any submissions, or if you wish, you could consider the matter and come back to the Chamber on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If Your Honour wouldn't mind if we could consider the matter. I have a feeling we won't have any further submissions. I believe the document is in evidence, so I don't think that there is much to comment on. But if I could just have a check, I would appreciate it, and come back tomorrow on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have any submissions to make on this, or would you rather wait until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would prefer to wait until tomorrow, given the submission that we have submitted to you relating to a medical document which, after we'd had discussion about it, was submitted to the Court. This document was put together much later, after the witness testified. For that reason, I would reserve my giving of any opinion until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. The next matter relates to the notification issued by the Trial Chamber on time allocation for the witnesses for this week. I believe the parties should be in possession of this communication. I turn next now to the matter which should be discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name, your place and date of birth for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Fikret Mujezinovic; 10th of October, 1945; Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to inform you that I am going to be asking you questions for about half an hour, so I'm going to try and be as succinct and brief as possible. I'm going to start by asking you questions about your background.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may I lead the witness through this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, is it correct that you presently live in Livanjska Street, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you live there during the war?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: During the war, is it correct that you were a cook for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I have photographs, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: During the war as well, is it true that you were a member of the veterans union? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of the veterans union; however, it was on their behalf that I distributed parcels to the families of those wounded and killed from the Kosevo Brdo territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And prior to the war you were an electrician and then you retired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you some questions about an incident that took place in Livanjska Street. But before I get there, I just want to ask some general questions about the area in which you lived. In Livanjska Street, in the area of Livanjska Street, during the war, were there any military facilities present?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: There was the military kitchen. That was further down the street. Now it's called Antuna Hangija and before it used to be called Mitra Trifunovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If you can very briefly describe to the Trial Chamber, what was the function of this military kitchen?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That's where meals were prepared for the soldiers who were deployed along the front lines surrounding Sarajevo. It would normally shut at 5.00 and open again at 1700 hours. Meals were prepared so that in the evening hours, between 2000 hours and 2400 hours, or by 5.00 in the morning when there was nobody out in the streets, meals could be distributed to the soldiers at the front lines. All the staff working there were wearing civilian clothes, and no one wearing a uniform was allowed anywhere near the kitchen, even those soldiers who would sometimes come back from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So can I just confirm from your answer there that the food, once it was made, was taken to the front lines, to the soldiers there, as opposed to the soldiers coming to the kitchen to eat in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was brought to the soldiers who were at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In addition to this -- well, apart from this military kitchen that we spoke about, were there any other military facilities in Livanjska Street during the period 1994/1995?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was the Red Cross kitchen at Livanjska Street. This kitchen was at Antuna Hangija Street and the school building was there. And down at the beginning of Livanjska Street, there was the police station. So those would be all the important facilities that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: During your -- well, during 1994/1995, did you ever see a heavy weapon or a mortar being used by the Bosnian government forces at Livanjska Street?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to move to an incident on the 8th of November, 1994. Firstly, if you could answer me, do you recall an incident taking place on that date?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I'll remember that for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court roughly what time this incident occurred on the 8th of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I will try to make this answer a little more comprehensive. That day at the Red Cross kitchen, which was where I worked, I had this office, the veterans association office, where they brought me parcels to distribute to the families of those wounded and killed. That day, at about 1500 hours, give or take a minute or two, a girl called Lejla Hodzic came over and said that her father had been killed, to see whether she could have the parcel. We weren't supposed to distribute those parcels during day-time because they could see us from the road over there. I told her that the parcels would be distributed after 6.00 and that she should drop by later. She went to see a lady over some books, because she had left school early because of the parcels. She went back to street number 26. The distance from the office was about 25 or 30 metres. I was just shuffling papers and then I heard this shell whizz by. It hit our building and I heard the impact. I had this knee-jerk reaction. I threw myself down on the floor and was waiting to see what would happen, because I realised that it had impacted very nearby. And then I jumped back up to my feet. I opened the door. I realised there was a lot of dust all around and shrapnel, shrapnel falling all over the ground. I dashed to the place where the shell exploded. It wasn't that far away. I saw this girl named Dino Blekic. She was squatting down, her arms raised. There was this cafe there at a distance of 2 metres with a passage that was leading to the building in which she lived. There's an intersection there, two cafes; one is called Dolar and the other, Maks. Some children were going close to Dolar and some other children, close to Maks. Between the buildings I ran there as fast as I could. Dina was holding her stomach as she lay down. Those other people who were closer to me, they were leaving Dolar and Maks; Djoko Miljkovic, Zdenko Jovanovic, Ragib Besic, Fikret Cerkez, and some other people whose names I can't remember. I saw them put him in a car, Dino, I mean. They put him in a car and I arrived just as they did. I knew that he was wounded, but I didn't know what would become of him. As I was approaching, to my right --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, I'm loathe to interpret you. I just want -- you've given a very long answer and I want to ask you a few specific questions about your answer and then we can continue to what you did at that time. Can I just ask you, you spoke about this girl Lejla who came to ask for packages. Do you recall roughly how old she was when you saw her that day?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Twelve, 13, 14. I wasn't really thinking about that. I know she was a lovely girl and she lived in this building where my daughter played with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered the question. You said she was 12, 13, or 14. Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also said in your answer, you say, this shell whizz by. Can you very briefly describe to the Court what you heard.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was like this: "Sssss, boom." A second was all it took. It just whizzed past and then it impacted. I knew it was close by because that wasn't the first one. Thousands have landed before. This whistle of a shell went whizzing past, and the impact. I heard a scream. I threw myself down on the floor. I didn't know where exactly it had landed and I thought the shrapnel might catch me, too, because before it hit a building in which I lived, near my room, which is just across the way from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I, for the record, describe the sound the witness made as a semi-whistle, I submit, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. Would you agree with that, Ms. Isailovic, that the sound was that of a semi-whistle?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all, because I heard in the witness's language it was a one-second whistle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, I suggest you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know if anything will turn on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, after the first shell landed, did you assist anybody who was injured from that shell?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Dino Blekic was put in a car. I ran over and then Adis Tinjak was also put in another car, and the car drove off. Only the little girl, Lejla Hodzic, was still there. And then Marin ran down the street and then the police caught him. He was wounded outside the entrance to that building. And my duty was to look after Lejla. I walked up to her. I lifted her up to put her in the car. I just lifted her up. I felt something warm under my fingers - I can still remember the feeling - and it was this little girl's brains. When we put her in the trunk of the car, I just zipped my jacket up. I put the remains of her brains in my jacket, and she was dead on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's okay, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Several minutes later, this lady that was taken out of an entrance at number 26, Ramiza, who was the owner of a burek shop, she told us that a lady was lying in the hall, a girl from that same building, wounded. Fikret Besic's daughters came in and they brought this lady out. Outside the entrance to her building there is a stone bench there. They laid her down on the bench. You couldn't really tell that she was wounded or anything, so we thought she was just fear-stricken and, as a result, that she had lost consciousness. I asked Ramiza to massage her breast a little, since she was a lady, too, and they fetched a glass of water from this cafe Maks. I walked up to her to try and open he mouth. I realised that her jaw was clenched tightly together and that the area around her mouth was turning blue. It was then that I realised that -- we stopped a man named Dzevad, who was a taxi driver before the war, we stopped his car and took her to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mujezinovic. I think you should elicit the evidence bit by bit, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, it's okay if you want to take a sip of water or take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you like a short break to compose yourself, Mr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you. I'm composed. I have gotten over the worst of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that the taxi driver took the lady to the hospital. Did you find out whether she survived this incident?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, she succumbed. Nena Deljanin, she succumbed. The doctors told her husband, who also worked at the hospital - he was an X-ray technician - they told him that this small piece of shrapnel had penetrated too far, and even if the doctors were right there, they couldn't have saved her. She left behind her son who was at the time perhaps 10 or 12 months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, after this incident, this shell, did anything else happen on that day?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Fifteen or 20 minutes later, this, what should I call it, arrived, the police in civilian clothes, led by Dragan Miokovic. The team came and they started taking photographs at the scene. They stopped us who had witnessed the incident; they took our names down. In the meantime, the French Battalion men had arrived. They tried to get the shell out of the ground. However, Dragan Miokovic, the inspector, did not allow them to do that before an on-site investigation took place. Their guide was a man named Miso who always smoked a pipe. He was their interpreter. They said that he would be there in 15 or 20 minutes. Since the police station was nearby, the place where it hit --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: -- was secured by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, and perhaps it was my fault for asking an open-ended question. But apart from this shell that we have spoken about, did any other shells land on Livanjska Street that day, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I'm trying to explain. The French Battalion left. These people were carrying out an on-site investigation and the police were securing the scene outside the school. They told the people back at the school that they should not allow any children outside. People were expecting another shell being fired, and this was just the time when children left school for the day. This policeman went down there and made sure that no children left the school building. Once the French Battalion men had left - and I'm probably losing track of this in terms of the time-line - the people who were controlling things, they took the measurements where the shell had come from. This took about one and a half hours, maybe two. I never thought that I would ever cross paths with any of those people. I didn't look at my watch. So another shell landed just behind us, and we were all assembled together outside the cafe that was called Dolar, waiting to see what would happen and awaiting reports. So the other shell landed just outside the entrance to the school building. Muharem Aladjuz, the policeman securing the spot, was wounded, and another lady, Razija Steta, Seta, was found dead near that corner, killed by a shell. And then several minutes later another shell landed across the way in the front yard of a private home, the distance being, I think, about 7, 8 or possibly 10 metres from the other one. So three shells landed within those two or three hours, and don't hold me to it. The time-line is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to say roughly how far the second shell was from the first shell when it landed?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Between the second and the third or between the first and the second?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right, between the first and the second.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Between the first and the second, the first landed by the gate to the Dolar cafe, between Maks and Dolar cafes; the second one landed on the concrete surface, some 30, 40 metres away, I don't know. And the distance between the second and the third was 7 or 8 metres, as wide as the road was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a photograph now and I'm going to ask you a few questions about the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Court Deputy, could we bring up 65 ter 2975.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, you should see a photograph on your screen shortly. Do you see a photograph on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What is that a photograph of, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That's the Maks cafe. That's the Dolar cafe. The shell landed here --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: -- and this is the entrance to number 26, and here's this concrete bench where Nena was lying before she was taken to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Mujezinovic, now you're going to have a marker pen, and I want you to listen very carefully to my questions and then I'm going to ask you to mark certain locations. So let's just try and do this one by one, just so that it's recorded properly. If you could first mark the cafe, the Dolar cafe, please, with a D, with the letter D.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Please also mark the Maks cafe with the letter M.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could you please also mark number 26 Livanjska Street with the letters -- with the figures 26.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In that photograph, do you see the place where you assisted the little girl, Lejla?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could you please put the letter L underneath that.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You also spoke about a lady that was injured and had to have a massage. Can you point out where that lady was assisted as well, if it's in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Here, on this bench, stone bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And her name was Deljanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Deljanin. First name Nena. I mean everybody called her Nena. I don't know what her real first name was, but her last name was Deljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. If you could put the letter N where you have marked that, please, just so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And lastly, are you able to see where the shell landed on that photograph, the first shell?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I have a problem with this car. Probably it's a little bit down the street, under this tree. Every year, on the anniversary of this incident, the owner of the Dolar cafe puts flowers here at this spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So could you put the letter S by the tree, then, please.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P283, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, now I just want to show you one last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could 65 ter 00084K be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, do you see a document in your language on the right-hand side of your screen?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see that on the top left-hand side corner it is -- it says that it's from the Ministry of the Interior, the security services centre, Sarajevo. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And does it appear to you to be a report in relation to the incident that you have just described to the Court?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look down the end of the first page.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want you to -- I want you to tell the Court whether you see a reference there to the girl, Lejla, that you assisted that afternoon on the 8th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. Dino Blekic was killed. Nevsija "Nena" Deljanin was killed. Cehajic was wounded, escaped, but then was caught. And the others I didn't see on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Where you say you've seen Dino Blekic -- you see where you see Dino Blekic? There's a paragraph just above that name. Do you see in that paragraph a reference to Lejla?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I see now. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what is the surname of this lady, Lejla.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Lejla Hodzic, living on Muhameda Dzudza 56. As far as I know, this is not correct, because my daughter, my son-in-law and my grandchildren lived in the same building as she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P284, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, do you wish to move on to another document afterwards? Have you finished with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, I don't know if you plan to ask the question I'm about to put. In this document, on the second paragraph, "Official Report," second paragraph, it is written here that the shell was fired from the aggressor's positions. The question I wanted to ask or put to the witness is the following: Witness, can you tell us which direction the shell came from, if you are able to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know this position very well. It came from the direction of Orlovac. For many years I was the caretaker of the hunter's lodge there and I passed through that area very often. And later it was established by the investigators, I believe, who did the measurements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shell fell in your street, didn't it? Was your house far removed or fairly close to the "aggressor's positions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Dolar cafe was on number 15. The kitchen where I was working was between 11 and 13, and the entrance to my building was right across; it was on number 12. So the distance between my building and the place where the shell landed was about 10 or 12 metres. This shell could not cause any damage because it fell behind my building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was your building quite a long ways away from the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, about -- I don't know which positions you're referring -- whose positions you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the paragraph I read "the aggressor's positions." Perhaps you could tell us something about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are other buildings in front of my building that have a direct view of the road that was constructed immediately before the war. It was constructed by the army. It was a detour leading to Vogosca and it was a ring around Sarajevo. So some 700 metres, as the crow flies, is my rough estimate. Don't take my word for it, but I don't think it's more than 700 metres. So this is the street that was connecting Vresa Bolivar [phoen], I don't know, Vogosca down there, and it ran around to Pale and onward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This is my last question, Witness: Your house, was it close to ABiH positions, the army, the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosnia-Herzegovina, let me tell you something -- well, the line where the BH army was was about 2 kilometres, and that is where the food was being taken to. So approximately 2 kilometres. I didn't measure it myself, but not more than 2 or 2.5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the examination-in-chief. Thank you, Mr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sachdeva. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Branislava Isailovic. I'm a lawyer attorney-at-law and I work for the Paris Bar Association. I defend Dragomir Milosevic. And I'm about to ask you a few questions which are related to what you have said today before the Trial Chamber. But I would also like to talk about what you have said on several occasions when you had interviews with the OTP. First of all, I'd like to ask you this question: You made several statements which I gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, I believe.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the statement you made on the 20th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an interview you had with the OTP on the 11th of November, 2002?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I probably do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the interview you had on the 27th of April, 2006? This was last year.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And after having come to The Hague on the 20th of February, you discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I just want to confirm. Counsel has spoken about an interview on the 11th of November, 2002. It is my understanding that it was the 11th of December, just for clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we have seen it. It's the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: After having come -- you came to The Hague and discussed matters with the Prosecutor on the 20th of February, 2007. Today you discussed the incident that took place on the 8th of November, 1994, and I will ask you a series of questions rather quickly. If you are able to answer the question, that's fine; otherwise, you can just say that you don't know. Did you hear an explosion, i.e., at 25 minutes past 3.00, something like a blow or a blast; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it, but it didn't last a second. A second is a short period of time. Let me explain to you, it was like, "Sssss, boom," and it lasts longer than a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: How many seconds?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It's ridiculous. I didn't measure seconds. I'm going to repeat it and you measure it yourself. I don't have time to do that and I'm not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: After that, around a quarter past 4.00 p.m., Policeman Miokovic came to that spot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. I didn't look at my watch. I only remember the time when Lejla came to my office. It was around 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: They came half an hour, 45 minutes, after the explosion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: After that, and you said a while ago, that the FreBat soldiers came to that location; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But before the arrival of FreBat, did you see any other UNPROFOR soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The FreBat soldiers left instantly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They came in a vehicle that we dubbed "frog." They wanted to dig out the shell. Investigator Miokovic didn't allow them to do so, and they said that they would be back after 20 minutes and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you stay all that time with the policeman? I'm thinking of Mr. Miokovic.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "The" policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And around half past 5.00, the police had finished with the investigation it was conducting at that location.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you said a few minutes ago that you were still there together with Mr. Miokovic and his team, if I understood you correctly, when the second shell fell approximately 30 to 40 metres away from the place the first shell had fallen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Miokovic was there, and the rest, they were waiting for the UNPROFOR to come, to extract the shell and take the measurements.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At half past 5.00, was it still light?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was dusk. It was not completely dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That same evening, did you watch the news that talked about this event?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, because we didn't have electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you live in Livanjska Street. Do you remember that on the next day Mr. Miokovic went, together with his team, to that spot?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him the following day. He may have come, but I don't know about the next day. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when did you get to know about the findings of the investigation conducted by Mr. Miokovic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about the investigation. A couple of days later, I was called to come to the former MUP of the republic. There was a young girl with long blonde hair and she was the first one to whom I gave a statement, and that is when I learned. After I'd given my statement, she told me that they had everything provided by the police who visited the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, on the 10th of November, 1994, you reported this to the police in Sarajevo; is that correct? Was it then that you discovered what the findings of the investigation conducted by the police were?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody notified me. The police were doing their job. They just asked me about my experience and about the knowledge that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, a few moments ago you said that this long-haired girl had told you something about the findings of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. The only thing that she told me was that an investigation had been carried out by Miokovic, Dragan Miokovic, the investigator. But she didn't impart any details on me, and it wasn't my place to ask anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement dated the 27th of April, 2006 --?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now is perhaps the time to display it on the screen. This is document DD00-0934.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the cover page of your witness statement -- of your statement?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: To the left-hand side of the screen, do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So can I therefore conclude that this is your statement?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to page 3 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to read it? I don't know if it's legible for you because the character font is quite small. Are you able to read this?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have two paragraphs that are numbered 13, so we have -- let's take the first paragraph 13, where you say: "Later on in the investigation by Dragan Miokovic and other UNPROFOR officials, it was confirmed that the shells originated from Orlovac."

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll put the question to you again. When did you discover the findings of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That same day. It was ascertained that the shell had come from Orlovac. All of us who were natives of the area knew exactly where Orlovac was, where Poljine was, where Barice was, where Mrkovici was. We were natives of the area. We knew that sort of thing. We also saw the way the shell hit the ground and it could have only come from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let us resume where we stopped, that is, paragraph 13 of your statement. You've already answered that question, but I would like to know when you heard about the results of the investigation conducted by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The same night. They were all there together. The interpreters were there. They discussed with the investigators, with Miokovic and those other people, and they must have agreed this because we were all there, all together, 15 or 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to your statement at a later stage, but I would like to talk about another document, which is the 65 ter document number 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is going to show and I would like to talk about the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we also have the translation of that document, but for the record, it is a technical report by Lieutenant-Colonel Lechevallier, Lieutenant-Colonel Reneric, and the UNMO team at an incident at Livanjska Street on the 8th of November, 1994. Witness, we have this document in front of us, and on page 3 you can see that UNPROFOR have come to the conclusion that it was most likely that the shell was coming from the territory under the control of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. Can you see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, indeed. Of course, there is no issue with respect to this document at this stage; however, I think it should be made clear that this document refers to the shelling that took place at, as it says on the front page, 1725 hours in the afternoon. In other words, it does not pertain to -- I mean, the witness has given evidence of three shells, the first one at sometime around 3.00 or thereafter in the afternoon. So it should be made clear to the witness that this relates to the shelling at 1725 hours on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are the other times that his evidence pointed to for the other shells?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The other shells were -- the evidence, as I understand it, were sometime after the first shell that landed at 3.00 or 3.30 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you are being asked to bear in mind that this report relates to a shelling that took place at 1725 hours, that is, 5.25. Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to use other documents which bear on the first incident, which pertain to the first incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But for the time being, Witness, what is your comment on this? Is it likely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what is the question? Are you asking him what are his comments on the conclusion that it was most likely that the shell came from territory under the control of the BH army? Is that what you're asking him? Okay. Yes. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You probably don't know the area. A street is like this and a shell came from here and the BH army were to the left. If the shell had arrived from BH army positions, it would have hit the ground like this and not like this. This way there was the army of Republika Srpska firing, and on this side there was the BH army. Had the army been fired at by the federation army, it would have come in like this. Since it had arrived from the Republika Srpska ranks, it came like this. When I close my eyes, I see in my mind's eye every second of it. I could perhaps go as far as to describe individual bits of shrapnel to you, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour, I would like to tender this technical report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D84, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you a question earlier but I would like to ask it again. The day after, you met Mr. Dragan Miokovic on the scene, that is, the 9th of November. You did see him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were at home in your office the day after, were you not?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, was I at home, was I in the office? I don't remember the next day. I came to the office at about 10.00, perhaps half past 10.00, when Nena Deljanin's husband arrived, crying, holding a small baby in his arms no more than 10 months old, to tell me that his wife had died the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember having seen on the scene the day after UNPROFOR soldiers or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just that day. They came again to that particular place three or four days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So have I understood that you can confirm the presence of UNPROFOR forces on the scene the day after the incident?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and they came later, too. They came every day. They even brought food that they distributed to children; eggs, soup, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show to the Chamber the 65 ter document number 63, and I would like page 5 to be shown. In the English version, it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, earlier on, the Prosecutor showed you a similar report. This is a report on incidents which took place in your street, Livanjska Street, on the 8th of November, and as you can read here, this is on incidents which took place slightly later, which you referred to as well. And you can see as well that it is Mr. Miokovic who conducted the investigation. Can you see that? Can you confirm that you can see that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could look at page number 6 for the B/C/S version and page 3 for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the English version, it is the final paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The final paragraph. Could you please zoom, yes. It goes on to the next page as well. It's the final paragraph for the B/C/S version, the very last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you can see that UNPROFOR went to the scene the day after to conduct investigations. Among those soldiers were Lieutenant-Colonel Reneric, and he was investigating, according to the report, on the first shell. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I haven't heard your answer. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender into evidence this report. It is number 63. It is a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you check whether this has already been tendered, Mr. Court Deputy. The Prosecutor shakes his head. Well, we admit it. We admit it. Would you just go back, Ms. Isailovic, and direct us to the part of the report which indicated where the shells came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not sure I understand your question. Is your question of this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This report, yes. I think just scroll -- scroll -- is it down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I saw a reference to the east and that's what caught my attention, so I'd like to find out where the east is in relation to the location and what forces were present in that direction. I think it is scrolling down. Is that being done by you or by your -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not my scrolling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's there now. It says: "It was determined that the shell had been fired from the east, from a direction 15 degrees due north-east, and that it was an 82-millimetre shell. The second shell came from the same direction and was of the same calibre." Is the witness able to tell us what, if any, forces were present in that area from which this report said the shell came, that is, from the east, and from a direction 15 degrees due north-east?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're showing me a different report, then. It doesn't say where the shell came from. It says: "When arriving for the on-site investigation of 9th November 1994, members of UNPROFOR were found on the spot who were already carrying out an on-site investigation where the shell had landed."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not the report we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I can help. In the report which is on our screens, in the B/C/S version I was drawing the witness's attention to this paragraph he's just read. I was doing so to confirm the presence of Lieutenant-Colonel Reneric the day after, the report of whom is tendered into evidence. Now, as regards the direction, it is another two paragraphs up the page, that is, page 3 of the report in English, and you can read there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that I saw and just read? Wasn't that part of the report or was that from a different document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are two reports, there are two Bosnian police reports, one of which is tendered by the Prosecutor -- excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, this document is relevant, because in Lieutenant-Colonel Reneric's report a time is stated, 1725, and in this Bosnian police document, it is said that there were another two shells and it is said that they find Lieutenant-Colonel Reneric on the spot, who's conducting his investigation on the first shell. So this is the reason why these are two separate incidents. But I think that we will hear the author of that report and we will discuss the matter with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Are you then preventing me from asking the question, Ms. Isailovic? It seems as if that is your intent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I would still like to find out, to get some information from the witness about that aspect of the report. If it is another report, then put it in context. But it was on the screen before us in court and caught my eye. So can we go back to the report that I referred to. Now, what is your submission on this report? Are you saying this is a report of a different incident, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. This is the incident which the witness mentioned. These were two shells that fell afterwards on the same spot, or a bit further away. But what is important to the Defence is that this report talks about the conditions in which the investigations were conducted by UNPROFOR. These findings figure in the UNPROFOR report, which is Exhibit D84. You probably remember Mr. Sachdeva's submission, and he was saying that this report was not related to the incident that occurred at 25 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, you testified about three incidents taking place that day, three shells. Can you tell us the time, roughly, when those three shells were fired? When was the first, when was the second, and when was the third?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first was at 13-something hundred hours. The ones we're looking at in this report, the first one is probably after 1800 hours. Somebody was looking at it; I wasn't. I didn't look at my watch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The first was at 1300 hours, approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was after 3.00 p.m., 15-something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean 1500, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 1500 hours, yes. And the second one was when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the two in the report, probably. I wasn't exactly watching the time. It must have been past 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Past 1800 hours, yes. And the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There, it's in the report. It's right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the third was when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the one that landed several minutes later, after the second one. It came from the same direction, same calibre, landed in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: About how many minutes later; 5, 10, 15, 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, when the third shell landed, we took Muharem away, who was wounded, and then another shell landed 10 minutes, 15 minutes. Muharem Aladjuz, the police officer, we took him away. Then later we found the body of that lady, Seta, or whatever her name was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So the report that I was looking at and which is before us now is a report which says that: "At about 6.00 on the 8th of November, opposite house number 36, a shell hit the road surface killing a woman, wounding another person. There was an inspection done of the site and it was determined that the shell had been fired from the east, from a direction 15 degrees due north-east." And so the question that I was asking you was: Are you able to tell us what forces, if any, would have been situated to the east of the location where the shell fell, where the shell hit the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's over to the other side, Spicaste Stijena, Vresa, Orlovac. It's like this: This is the street, and then to the right, up in the hills, the forces of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And are you able to say whether that area would have been occupied exclusively by the forces of the Serb army or whether there were other forces from the Bosnian Muslim side there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not there. The BH army were to the left, and they were lower down at the foot, not up in the hills. It was the Serbian army who were in the hills, and the Bosnian army were at the foot. They dug up trenches to keep those people up in the hills from descending. The Bosnian army were not in the hills; they did not hold any positions in the hills at the time. At the time there, the greatest elevation was near Poljine. So we were looking this way. And it was more of a meadow, really, than anything. But that was opposite the side being shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we have an exhibit number, please, for this 65 ter document, which is number 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as Exhibit D85.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We shall now discuss the statement you gave, your statement of the 27th of April, which is number DD00-0934.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the statement on the screen. I'm sure you remember we have -- we had two paragraphs that were numbered paragraph 13. Now, if you would allow me, I'd like to turn to the second paragraph number 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It was later confirmed by investigations done by Dragan Miokovic of the police and other UNPROFOR officials that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please wait for the interpretation to be finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't read this second paragraph 13. You don't have to read it aloud. Just read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I read it and maybe I can read it for the benefit of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The Bench already has the document. They have the English version of this document on their screen. Witness, you mentioned this kitchen which provided for the ABiH army which was close by. Can we agree that in order to fetch food the military trucks needed to go to this place?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not on Livanjska Street. It was an entrance from the other side. As you can see, from the upper side of number 17, from Mitra Trifunovica Uce Street, which is now called Antuna Hangija Street. So that's from the upper side. It used to be a kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we shall look at the map on the screen a little later on and you will be able to indicate it to us on the map. But just one question which relates to your statement: You say that the people who were working there were not wearing uniforms but were wearing civilian clothes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, these people were members of the army; no?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: There were no women. There was just one cook.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The people who came to fetch the food, were they also dressed in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was driven by two couriers who went in the evening in cars and in civilian clothes and drove the vans with the food. Their lights were out in order for them not to be able observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the case manager to display this Sarajevo street map, which is a 65 ter document, number 2872. In the meantime, I would like to tender this statement into evidence, please, DD00-0934.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D86, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have the right-hand side of the map enlarged, please. The right-hand side. If we could zoom in a little more, please. It's that corner I'm interested in. If you could enlarge it as much as possible, please. I'd like the witness to mark this map, if he can be given the electronic pen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see your street on this map?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Zoom in a little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It went the other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move the map to the right, please. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's perfect now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little. Can we scroll down as far as Miljacka. No, scroll down. Down. Go down to Miljacka. More. More. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now show us where it is, please.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What are you interested in?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show us where your street is, please.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the street Brace Begic. It runs as far as Ukiceva. This is where the Red Cross was, this is where I live, and this is the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark it with an L which stands for "Livanjska," please.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now the street is called Brace Begic, I believe, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this map be marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D87, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like my case manager to display map number 2927; it's a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Let me explain to you this map. This is a very nice map. Let me explain where the entrance to the military kitchen was, if you would allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are only interested in matters that are relevant, so I'm not sure whether that is a matter in which we are interested. Are you interested in that, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not really, but we can compare the transcript with the evidence we have in front of us. And he did say that the kitchen and the Red Cross was located in such-and-such a place, but if he so wishes, he can show us where the entrance to the kitchen was and he can mark this with the letter C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us do so quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thank the Defence for allowing me to do this. This is the Brace Begic Street, already marked. This is Antuna Hangija Street and this is the entrance to the army kitchen. And here, where there's -- where the cross is and the letter S, that was the Red Cross. So Brace Begic Street has no connection with the kitchen. And this letter S here indicates a school. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm putting the question to the court officer: Is this Exhibit 87? Can we keep that number or can't we? So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I just want to -- just to be clear, the witness marked the location of the Red Cross and I see -- at least in my eyes it's a letter C and the transcript reads the letter S. I just don't want there to be any confusion. Because just below the C there's also the B/C/S letter "Sh," which looks like an S in English, but I just want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did you ask the witness to mark? What did you ask the witness to mark, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness wanted to indicate where the entrance to the military kitchen was, which is what he did. But then he added on an S to indicate where the school was. I didn't ask him to do so, but he did. He added on the S to show where the school was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. So the S stands for school?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But there is a letter C at the top, and from my reading of the transcript, that relates to the Red Cross kitchen and not the military kitchen. Just so there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll just ask the witness: The place you have marked with the letter C, what kitchen does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letter C indicates the Red Cross kitchen. And on the upper side, from Antuna Hangija Street, I put the letter V, which stands for military kitchen. And a little bit below that is it a letter "Sh," or S, indicating a school. And the former Livanjska Street is now called Brace Begic Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the map on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, 45 minutes have passed, which is what was allotted to you, but I'll allow you some more time, in view of the time spent by the Bench in questioning. Another 10/15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's going to be faster than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see this map in front of you, and do you know anything about maps? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It's too small for me to find my way around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall ask the court officer to enlarge the right-hand side of the map, please, where you can read the letters "105 bbr." Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see a little better? Can you see where Miljacka is, and from then on, can you see where your street stands?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It's really difficult for me to see anything here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see Miljacka?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's down here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you the Kosevo stadium?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm precisely looking for it in order to help me orientate. Believe me, I cannot find my way around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's move on. He cannot help you with the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I shall finish now. I wanted to ask a few questions about the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I just have one last question: Did you know where the confrontation line was close to where you were?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that it was somewhere in Poljine, but I didn't know the exact location. I never went there. My concern was the Red Cross kitchen where I had my team with whom I prepared three meals a day for everyone, regardless of their religion, their ethnicity, and all the other poor people in the hills. We prepared between 600, 700 meals; my team and I did that, and therefore I had no time to look around and see where everything was. If you wish, I can only show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that you're desiring to show us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To show you a photograph of my team of cooks. We didn't have time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's very nice, but let us move on. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You know what your job is. Thank you very much for allowing me to get it off my chest, what I have been suffering from, in the name of the children and all other people who suffered. Thank you, and I appreciate this Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I be excused for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit. And you may begin, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you feeling relaxed?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Pretty well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: You want me to tell you my name?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Azra Sisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where did you live in 1995?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: In Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in which street?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: It was called Marka Oreskovica at the time. Now it's called Mustafika --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the name of the street, how it's called today?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Mustafika Kamenica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I briefly want to discuss the situation of living as it was in 1995 in Dobrinja. Can you tell the Judges whether you had access to food and perhaps to humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Already in that year the supply of food was kind of orderly. We received humanitarian aid on a regular basis, and as for other events, it was horrible. There was a lot of shelling. Snipers were shooting. There was a lot of killing and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in terms of food, where did you have to go to get it?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Well, it was organised in such a way that each floor had a duty warden, or sort of, and I sometimes was assigned this duty. These persons had to go 100 or 200 metres away from the building and it was a risky business.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why was it risky?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Because of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How was the water situation? How were you able to get water for your family?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: We didn't have either water or electricity or gas. It was scarcely supplied to our flats. There were pumps all over Dobrinja, and most often they were targets of the shellings. And there were also one or two wells in the neighbourhood, so my husband often went out during the night to bring water.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why would he go at night to get water?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Because during the day there was sniper activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One of these wells you were talking about, or pumps, was it at the Simone Bolivar school in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a pump there. The well was a little bit further on. I never went to this well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how far away was the Simone Bolivar school from your home?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: It was pretty close. There was just a playground between my house and the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was it -- you said earlier that it was dangerous to venture outside your apartment. How was it to get from your home to the Simone Bolivar school where the water station was located?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to virtually fly across this playground. We had to run because snipers were shooting in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know where the snipers were shooting from?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know that they were in Nedzarici, which is a neighbourhood nearby. So I assume they were shooting from there, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know who controlled Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: The Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in order to protect you from the sniping activities, were there barriers erected near the school?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the C5 neighbourhood behind the school and there was sniping activity along that street. Containers were set up to protect people and people would just try to cross the street, running as fast as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Going back to the Simone Bolivar school, was it in operation during -- in 1995? Was it -- you know, was school held for children?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: No. Their schools were set up in basements across town. The school building itself was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know when it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: In the earlier days of the war, it was shelled and it caught fire. Men from the surrounding buildings tried to put the fire out, but there was so much sniping activity that it simply wasn't possible. I think a man was even killed in the attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me, very briefly, go to your apartment. Was it safe for you to stay in your apartment all the time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA SISIC
utterances.text: No, no, not early on. Whoever had flats facing the school, for as long as the Serbs were at the airport, so that was the side facing the airport, that was dangerous.
